16	## Section A — Reconstruction (first three of eight stories, in chronological order)

18	### 1. The Founding, the Station, and the Fatal Purchase (1889–1897)
19	
20	In 1889, valley farmers weary of hauling their butter all the way to Ashlin met at the Larrow Green
21	schoolhouse and organized the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association. They elected Gideon
22	Vose — "a heavy, quiet, obstinate man who had once thought of the law and thought better of it" —
23	as first president; he wrote the Association's by-laws himself, at his own kitchen table. This
24	comes from Dell Rundle's 1939/1959 jubilee pamphlet, "The Larrow Valley Creamery: Fifty Years," the
25	main secondary history of the founding.
26	
27	In 1891 the Association built its creamery at Larrow Green, on the creek below the mill, and began
28	paying the valley in cash monthly for the first time. Rundle, quoting the text directly, dates
29	Article VII of the by-laws to that same year: every patron would be paid according to the butterfat
30	test of the station where he delivered, not the weight of his milk — later called "the hinge of the
31	whole matter." A single secondhand 1919 letter suggests 1893 instead, but only as a vague
32	recollected impression ("as I have always understood it"), so the 1891 dating, resting on a quoted
33	document, is preferred.
34	
35	On 4 May 1896 — the most precise date, from county agent Orin Falke's 1959 report, matched loosely
36	by buttermaker Hobart Sill's own 1934 recollection of "May 1896" — the Association opened a second
37	station at Ostrey Hollow, seven miles up the valley (three independent narrators agree on "seven"),
38	serving the Hessel Bottom farms. Ansel Keddie was appointed tester and separator man there, a post
39	he held for 29 unbroken seasons, to 1925. The station opened with no testing glass of its own; Sill
40	lent his own outfit from Larrow Green for its first season.
41	
42	The station's own glassware arrived on 1 May 1897 — the best-supported of four rival dates (1897,
43	1898, 1899, 1922), corroborated by a supplier's invoice, that supplier's own company history, and a
44	tester's-wife's diary. The invoice, dated 14 April 1897, itemizes six dozen milk-test pipettes,
45	twelve dozen test bottles, an acid measure, and a hand tester; the line items total $77.93, though
46	the supplier's own prose gives $77.39 — an unresolved discrepancy inside that one source. This
47	unremarkable purchase turned out to be the origin of a defect that went undetected for the next 26
48	years.
49
